newsitem.title: UK: WORLD BONDS-T-notes to withstand payroll onslaught.
newsitem.headline: WORLD BONDS-T-notes to withstand payroll onslaught.

text.p: U.S. Treasuries will stand their ground in the face of Friday's key payrolls data and investors can even look forward to some spread narrowing with Bunds, analysts said on Thursday.
But the prospect of further U.S. interest rate hikes will temper any gains and leave the market subject to volatility over the next few months.
"There is potential for the market to squeeze higher if the figures on Friday are O.K.," said Graham McDevitt, head of bond research at Paribas Capital Markets in London.
He said the market had 70 percent discounted a further rate hike, which together with Wall Street jitters, meant the front end of the U.S. curve had been better bid recently.
According to a Reuters poll, economists expect March non-farm payrolls, due at 1330 GMT on Friday, to rise by 182,000, down from February's 339,000 rise.
Average hourly earnings are seen up 0.4 percent following February's 0.2 percent rise and unemployment is expected to edge down 0.10 percent to 5.2 percent.
McDevitt said the crucial number from the labour data would be the earnings component.
"The key is earnings. The economy has been growing above trend for some time, so the reason the Fed will hike again is increased inflation risk," he said.
Markets have braced themselves for a further hike in U.S. interest rates ever since the 25 basis point increase in the federal funds target rate to 5.50 percent on March 25.
A statement by the Fed at the time said it tightened credit because persistent strength in demand was progressively increasing the risk of inflationary imbalances in the economy.

Stephen Lewis, director of research at London Bond Broking, said Treasuries' recent resilience in the face of some fairly robust economic data, reflected the market's perception that monetary tightening this time round was simply fine tuning.

"If the payrolls data tomorrow is above market expectations, it will be seen as pertaining to the first quarter -- the market will be asking what's going to happen in the second quarter," he said. "So if it's rather strong, the yield may tick up a few basis points, but we will likely see buyers at that level."

Lewis said the 30-year yield would likely be capped at around 7.15 percent. "And until we know what the Fed is going to do at the FOMC on May 20, I don't see the 30-year yield dropping much below 6.80 percent," he said.
By 1000 GMT, the benchmark long-bond was at 94-08 to yield 7.08 percent.
Lewis said the 10-year T-note/Bund spread would likely narrow slightly, but more because of slipping Bunds, rather than strong Treasuries.
Nigel Richardson, head of bond research at Yamaichi International here, said he was optimistic about the data.
"But any upside for the market will be temporary relief until we get the next rate move out of the way," he said.
If there was any near term respite, he said it would probably be in the 10-year area and possibly the long end.
Lewis agreed that on a three-month view, the 30-year offered best value. But shorter term, he favoured the five year area, which he said was cheapest in terms of normal yield curve shape.
McDevitt was more optimistic for the shorter end.
"The front end is the place to be at the moment, there's too much directional risk at the long end, so I'd be in the two to three year area," he said.
He said the 10-year T-note/Bund spread would range between 80-100 basis points and be volatile in the next three months.

"But on a six to 12 month view, that spread will head towards flat, as the U.S. economy slows down and Germany speeds up. So we recommend using weakness in the Treasury market to buy Treasuries and switch out of core Europe," he said.
